slides.teacher_cue: Same spelling — different sound. oo can say /ʊ/ (short) as in book, cook, look. Lips are rounded but less tightly than /uː/. The sound is shorter and lower. This is one of the trickiest English spelling facts: oo has two sounds. Context and vocabulary knowledge help. Contrast: moon /uː/ — book /ʊ/. food /uː/ — good /ʊ/. spoon /uː/ — cook /ʊ/.
slides.expected_response: Students produce short /ʊ/ and understand that oo can represent either /uː/ or /ʊ/.
slides.correction_move: Model the contrast pairs: moon/book, food/good, spoon/cook. Students hear and repeat. Emphasise that both spellings are oo — context determines which sound.
slides.observation_note: Watch for /uː/ substitution — students will default to the previously taught sound. This ambiguity is a feature of English to be managed, not an error in the programme.

content_payload.correction_routine: book has /ʊ/; moon has /uː/. Same spelling, different vowel sound.

slides.teacher_cue: Play both words. Ask students to choose the short oo word and explain the difference from long oo.
slides.expected_response: Students identify book as short oo and reject moon as long oo.
slides.correction_move: Rehearse both words with hand motions: short for /ʊ/, long stretch for /uː/.
slides.observation_note: Watch for carryover from the previous lesson where students default oo to /uː/.
